questions.worked_solution:
To compute $P(B|A),$ we need to ask, "what is the probability of $B$ occurring given that $A$ has occurred?"

Since we are assuming that $A$ has occurred, we only consider the events inside $A.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273146/assets/56a6299b9db053fe3ab235c2cc98f7dfdb849beb37d3f2987026a6f89aa4191b.png)

The probability of event $A$ occurring is

$$
P(A)=0.2+0.05=0.25.
$$

Now, $P(B|A)$ can be interpreted as the proportion of $B$ that lies inside $A,$ relative to the size of $A.$ So, we have

$$
P(B|A)=\frac{0.05}{0.25}=0.2.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We wish to compute the probability that a singer is a rock singer *given that* he/she is a pop singer. Therefore, we need to compute $P(R|P).$ 

To compute $P(R|P),$ we need to ask, "what is the probability of $R$ occurring given that $P$ has occurred?"

Since we are assuming that $P$ has occurred, we only consider the singers inside $P.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273146/assets/d4b01d31b2aa39da2878709417fdc4a348f981f1ce4c2bf3faa40ad6505dc037.png)

In total, the number of singers in the set $P$ is 

$$

$$

Of these $34$ singers, $22$ lie inside $R.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273146/assets/e24ab4d3a89d73e3cf41fbe294d744be4ad100e95d18ee93ea7ba8d442ae3f9a.png)

Since each outcome is equally likely, $P(R|P)$ can be interpreted as the proportion of $R$ that lies inside $P,$ relative to the size of $P.$ Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(R|P) & =\frac{22}{34}=\frac{11}{17}.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we have surveyed $100$ students regarding their sports preferences, asking them whether they like baseball or volleyball. The results of our survey are shown in the Venn diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273146/assets/8256ef61b286b139cfb4bc0c7305e3f6f1fd1795321799e36a446fb409e1621e.png)

Now, suppose that we wish to calculate the probability that a randomly selected student who likes volleyball also likes baseball. We represent this probability symbolically as

$$
P(\textrm{ student likes baseball } | \textrm{ student likes volleyball }).
$$

Said in words, we would read the above as "the probability that a student likes baseball **given that** they like volleyball." This type of probability is called a **conditional probability.** In this case, we can think of this probability as the proportion of volleyball-liking students who also like baseball.

Since we assume that the student likes volleyball, we only need to look at the area of the Venn diagram that is inside the right-hand circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273146/assets/cf5f6469d01a23774575f37e1f5f167fc377b42de2589fd15e201bae1ecfe591.png)

In total, the number of students who like volleyball is

$$
30+20=50.
$$

Of these $50$ students, only $30$ of them also like baseball. This is represented by the area where the circles $A$ and $B$ overlap.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273146/assets/fb044e942e1e27edbc162df95925d7e22b190112eeccdaca06cd713d1ef145d0.png)

Therefore, the probability that a randomly selected student likes baseball *given that* they like volleyball, is

$$
P(\textrm{ student likes baseball } | \textrm{ student likes volleyball }) =  \dfrac{30}{50} = \dfrac35.
$$

This type of probability is called a **conditional probability.** In this case, we can think of this probability as the proportion of volleyball-liking students who also like baseball.

Since we assume that the student likes volleyball, we only need to look at the area of the Venn diagram that is inside the right-hand circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273146/assets/cf5f6469d01a23774575f37e1f5f167fc377b42de2589fd15e201bae1ecfe591.png)

In total, the number of students who like volleyball is

$$
30+20=50.
$$

Of these $50$ students, only $30$ of them also like baseball. This is represented by the area where the circles $A$ and $B$ overlap.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14273146/assets/fb044e942e1e27edbc162df95925d7e22b190112eeccdaca06cd713d1ef145d0.png)

Therefore, the probability that a randomly selected student likes baseball *given that* they like volleyball, is

$$
P(\textrm{ student likes baseball } | \textrm{ student likes volleyball }) =  \dfrac{30}{50} = \dfrac35.
$$
